thing: Smartphone-based social media (Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok) for adolescents
claim: Social media use is driving a surge in teen depression, anxiety and self-harm, especially among girls.
what_happened: Meta's own 2019-2020 research found Instagram worsened body image for a third of teen girls and the US Surgeon General issued a 2023 advisory, but meta-analyses (Odgers, Orben, Vuorre-Przybylski 72-country study) find small or mixed associations and no proof social media caused the population-level crisis.
dismissed_by: Meta publicly (Zuckerberg) and, on the causal claim, developmental psychologists Candice Odgers and Amy Orben
cost_of_error: Contested; Meta faces suits from 40+ US state attorneys general (2023) over youth harm, and teen girl depression and self-harm rates roughly doubled 2010-2020 with cause unresolved.
lesson: A product's own internal research showing harm to a subgroup is real evidence even when population-level causation stays unproven; plan for the subgroup harm, not the headline debate.

quotes.text: we make body issues worse for one in three teenage girls
quotes.speaker: Facebook internal Instagram researchers (as reported in the Wall Street Journal's Facebook Files)

quotes.text: the book’s repeated suggestion that digital technologies are rewiring our children’s brains and causing an epidemic of mental illness is not supported by science.
quotes.speaker: Candice L. Odgers

thing: Mechanical dial switching replacing human telephone switchboard operators (AT&T)
claim: Automatic dial switching would wipe out telephone operating, then one of the commonest jobs for American women.
what_happened: Automation eliminated most operator jobs in cities that converted 1920-1940 and incumbent operators a decade later were more likely in lower-paying work or out of the labour force, but future cohorts of young women saw no drop in overall employment as clerical and service jobs absorbed them.
dismissed_by: AT&T and the later economic consensus that aggregate employment adjusts
cost_of_error: Incumbent operators bore the loss (downward mobility or exit); the IBEW Telephone Operators' Department lost much of its membership after 1923, partly to dial conversion; no aggregate employment loss for later cohorts.
lesson: Automation fears are usually right about the incumbents who hold the job today and wrong about the aggregate, so the question for a decision is whose job, not how many jobs.

thing: Automobiles, motor trucks and tractors replacing the horse
claim: The horseless carriage would ruin the trades built around the horse: blacksmiths, teamsters, liverymen, stable hands, harness and carriage makers.
what_happened: US census counts collapsed within two decades: blacksmiths fell from about 233,000 (1910) to 124,365 (1930), draymen, teamsters and carriage drivers from about 444,000 to 111,224, and hostlers and stable hands from 63,382 to 6,654, while chauffeurs and truck drivers rose to 972,418.
dismissed_by: Those who treated the motor car as a rich man's fad that would never displace the horse
cost_of_error: Roughly 450,000 horse-trade jobs gone 1910-1930 across blacksmiths, teamsters and stable hands alone; the trades never recovered, though motor-vehicle jobs more than replaced them in aggregate.
lesson: When a technology replaces the power source an entire service economy is built around, the dependent trades do not shrink, they vanish, and fast; the question is only whether you are the blacksmith or the garage.

thing: Power looms, wide stocking frames and cropping machines in English textiles
claim: Textile machinery would throw skilled weavers, stockingers and croppers out of work and into starvation.
what_happened: Right for the workers who made it: as the power loom spread 1800-1820 handloom weavers went from earning twice a factory worker's wage to 25% less and the trade died out over the following decades, while economy-wide real wages stayed flat into the 1820s; wrong about the long run, as mechanised textiles later underwrote rising wages and far more employment.
dismissed_by: Parliament and mill owners, who made machine-breaking a capital crime in the Frame Breaking Act of 1812
cost_of_error: Handloom weavers' relative wage fell from 2x to 0.75x a factory worker's by 1820 and kept falling; a generation of Britain's most numerous skilled trade was impoverished, with men hanged and transported for machine-breaking.
lesson: The Luddites were right about their own lives and wrong about the century; a productivity shock can raise the long-run pie while destroying the incumbents' share for a whole working lifetime.

quotes.text: These machines were to them an advantage, inasmuch as they superseded the necessity of employing a number of workmen, who were left in consequence to starve. By the adoption of one species of frame in particular, one man performed the work of many, and the superfluous labourers were thrown out of employment.
quotes.speaker: Lord Byron, maiden speech in the House of Lords
quotes.publication: History of Information (from R. C. Dallas, Recollections of the Life of Lord Byron, 1824)

thing: Personal smartphones carried into school classrooms
claim: Smartphones in class wreck students' attention and learning, so schools should ban them.
what_happened: OECD PISA 2022 found students distracted by classmates' devices scored 15 maths points lower (about three-quarters of a year of schooling) and heavy leisure users 49 points lower, but the 2025 SMART Schools study of 30 English schools found restrictive phone bans cut in-school use without improving wellbeing or total use.
dismissed_by: Ed-tech advocates and permissive school policies treating phones as learning tools
cost_of_error: Correlational: a 15-point PISA maths gap for distracted students, with 65% of students across the OECD distracted by devices in at least some maths lessons; bans themselves show no measured wellbeing gain.
lesson: A harm can be real while the obvious fix does nothing measurable; separate evidence that the product hurts from evidence that the proposed restriction helps.

quotes.text: Students who reported being distracted by other students using digital devices in some, most or every maths class scored 15 points lower in PISA maths tests than those who barely experienced this.
quotes.speaker: OECD

quotes.text: There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents.
quotes.speaker: Victoria A. Goodyear et al.

thing: State-legalised sports betting, especially mobile apps, after Murphy v. NCAA (2018)
claim: Legal sports betting would be the largest gambling expansion in US history and drive a wave of gambling problems and hidden social costs.
what_happened: Credit-panel studies of millions of consumers found that in states permitting online betting, bankruptcy filing likelihood rose 25-30%, debt-collection amounts 8%, card and auto delinquencies about 8%, and credit scores fell; magnitudes were revised across versions (a later draft put bankruptcies near +10%) and an industry-friendly think tank disputes it, but the direction has held into a Management Science publication.
dismissed_by: State legislatures and sportsbook operators selling tax revenue, plus a Progressive Policy Institute report finding no bankruptcy rise
cost_of_error: Roughly 30,000 additional US bankruptcies a year by the authors' later estimate, plus higher collections and delinquencies concentrated among low-savings households; over half a trillion dollars wagered.
lesson: When a product moves a known addictive behaviour onto a phone with frictionless deposits, assume the harm shows up in credit files within a few years and price it in.

quotes.text: Today’s ruling could set the stage for what might be the largest simultaneous expansion of regulated gambling in U.S. history.
quotes.speaker: Tristyn Eppley, President of the Problem Gambling Network of Ohio (NCPG affiliate)
quotes.publication: Pause Before You Play / PGNO press release

quotes.text: In states allowing online sports gambling, the likelihood of a personal bankruptcy filing rose 25% to 30% in the years after legalization, the data suggests.
quotes.speaker: UCLA Anderson Review, summarising Hollenbeck, Larsen and Proserpio

thing: Face search across photos scraped from the open web (Clearview AI)
claim: Facial recognition matched against public internet photos is too dangerous to release because it lets anyone identify and track strangers.
what_happened: Google withheld the capability in 2011, but Clearview AI built it anyway from tens of billions of scraped images, sold it to police and agencies, and was ruled unlawful by multiple European regulators, including a €30.5M Dutch fine (2024) and a £7.5M UK fine (2022), while settling US privacy class actions.
dismissed_by: Clearview AI and the police departments that adopted it, arguing public photos are fair game
cost_of_error: At least four national fines including €30.5M (Netherlands) and £7.5M (UK), largely unpaid, plus orders to delete data; a database of more than 70 billion faces built without consent.
lesson: When the incumbent that can build a capability chooses not to for safety reasons, expect a smaller, less constrained entrant to build it, and expect regulators to arrive only after the database exists.

quotes.text: We actually built that technology and we withheld it,
quotes.speaker: Eric Schmidt, Google executive chairman, at All Things Digital D9

quotes.text: ‘Facial recognition is a highly intrusive technology, that you cannot simply unleash on anyone in the world’, Dutch DPA chairman Aleid Wolfsen says.
quotes.speaker: Aleid Wolfsen, chairman, Dutch Data Protection Authority

thing: Post-9/11 NSA bulk collection of Americans' phone records and communications under secret Patriot Act and FISA interpretations
claim: The government was secretly reading the Patriot Act to authorise mass domestic surveillance of Americans' communications records.
what_happened: Snowden's 2013 documents confirmed bulk collection of Americans' phone metadata under Section 215, as Senator Wyden and NSA whistleblowers William Binney and Thomas Drake had warned; in 2015 the Second Circuit held the program exceeded what Congress authorised, and Congress ended bulk collection in the USA Freedom Act.
dismissed_by: DNI James Clapper ('No, sir... Not wittingly', March 2013) and NSA Director Keith Alexander, who called the dossier claims 'absolute nonsense'
cost_of_error: Years of unlawful collection (Stellar Wind recorded 320 million calls a day at the outset by Binney's account), a DNI's misleading Senate testimony, and a 2015 appellate ruling that the program violated Section 215.
lesson: When an insider with clearance says publicly that the secret interpretation differs from the public text, and officials answer with categorical denials rather than specifics, the insider is usually right.

quotes.text: The fact is that anyone can read the plain text of the Patriot Act, and yet many members of Congress have no idea how the law is being secretly interpreted by the executive branch, because that interpretation is classified. It's almost as if there were two Patriot Acts, and many members of Congress have not read the one that matters.
quotes.speaker: Sen. Ron Wyden, Senate floor speech

claim: YouTube's recommender pushes viewers toward ever more extreme content, making it a mass radicalisation engine.
what_happened: YouTube changed its recommender in 2019 to demote borderline content; later audit and panel studies (Chen, Nyhan et al., Science Advances 2023) found no broad rabbit-hole effect after the change, with extremist viewing concentrated among already-resentful users who subscribe or arrive via external links, though the platform still hosts and serves that audience.
dismissed_by: YouTube, and later empirical researchers who found demand-driven rather than algorithm-driven exposure
cost_of_error: Unquantified; the pre-2019 period is poorly measured, and the post-2019 evidence shows extremist exposure concentrated in a small resentful minority rather than mass conversion.
lesson: A loud public warning can be partly self-defeating, prompting the fix that makes later studies find no effect, so judge such fears on the system as it stood when the warning was made.

quotes.text: Given its billion or so users, YouTube may be one of the most powerful radicalizing instruments of the 21st century.
quotes.speaker: Zeynep Tufekci, New York Times op-ed 'YouTube, the Great Radicalizer'
quotes.publication: Benton Institute (excerpt of New York Times)

quotes.text: Our findings suggest that YouTube’s algorithms were not sending people down “rabbit holes” during our observation window in 2020, possibly due to changes that the company made to its recommender system in 2019.
quotes.speaker: Annie Y. Chen, Brendan Nyhan, Jason Reifler, Ronald E. Robertson, Christo Wilson

thing: App-based ride-hail driving as independent contract work (Uber, Lyft)
claim: Ride-hail driving pays far less than advertised once costs are counted, shifting risk onto drivers as contractors.
what_happened: The FTC found Uber had advertised median uberX incomes of over $90,000 in New York and $74,000 in San Francisco when the real gross medians were $61,000 and $53,000, and Uber paid $20M in 2017; an MIT CEEPR estimate of $3.37 median hourly profit was walked back after Uber's critique, but the revision still left about 41-54% of drivers earning below their state minimum wage after expenses, while other studies find higher pay and drivers valuing flexibility.
dismissed_by: Uber's own recruiting claims and early company-commissioned studies of driver pay
cost_of_error: $20M FTC settlement for exaggerated earnings and car-financing claims; fewer than 10% of drivers in New York and San Francisco earned the touted income, and Uber's leasing program left drivers with worse rates than comparable borrowers.
lesson: When a platform recruits labour with headline earnings, ask for the net-of-cost median, because the gap between the advertised number and that one is where the worker's risk lives.

quotes.text: The FTC alleges, however, that drivers’ annual median income was actually $61,000 in New York and $53,000 in San Francisco.
quotes.speaker: Federal Trade Commission

thing: Industrially formulated ultra-processed foods (NOVA group 4) dominating the diet
claim: The degree of industrial processing itself, not just nutrients, is driving obesity and chronic disease.
what_happened: A 2024 BMJ umbrella review of 45 pooled analyses covering about 9.9 million people found direct associations with 32 of 45 outcomes, rated convincing for cardiovascular death, type 2 diabetes, anxiety and common mental disorders, but most evidence was graded low or very low quality on GRADE and the NOVA category remains contested as too broad to identify a mechanism.
dismissed_by: Food industry groups and nutrition scientists who argued processing is not a meaningful causal category apart from salt, sugar, fat and calories
cost_of_error: Associations of about 50% higher cardiovascular-disease death risk and 12% higher type 2 diabetes risk per dose increment, applied to a food category that dominates calorie intake in rich-country diets.
lesson: A warning framed around a new category can be directionally right well before the mechanism is proven; act on consistent associations at population scale, but expect the category's boundaries to be fought over.

quotes.text: Nutrition and health. The issue is not food, nor nutrients, so much as processing.
quotes.speaker: Carlos A. Monteiro
quotes.publication: Public Health Nutrition (title, via Europe PMC record PMID 19366466)

quotes.text: Greater exposure to ultra-processed food was associated with a higher risk of adverse health outcomes, especially cardiometabolic, common mental disorder, and mortality outcomes.
quotes.speaker: Melissa M. Lane et al.

thing: Permanent normal trade relations with China (2000) and China's WTO entry (2001)
claim: Opening US markets permanently to Chinese imports would unleash an import surge that destroys American manufacturing jobs.
what_happened: Autor, Dorn and Hanson's China Shock research found that in exposed local labour markets wages and labour-force participation stayed depressed and unemployment elevated for at least a decade, exposed workers lost lifetime income, and national employment in exposed industries fell without offsetting gains elsewhere, overturning the economists' consensus that labour markets adjust quickly to trade.
dismissed_by: The Clinton administration, most trade economists and business groups, who argued the deal opened China to US exports and that displaced workers would be reabsorbed
cost_of_error: Net US job losses of 2.0 to 2.4 million from Chinese import competition 1999-2011 (Acemoglu, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Price), with wages, participation and employment depressed for a decade in exposed regions.
lesson: Aggregate-gains arguments are usually right about the national total and wrong about how long a concentrated local shock takes to heal, so ask where the losses land and how mobile those workers really are.

quotes.text: American workers, including thousands of UAW members in the automotive and aerospace industries, have not been protected against a surge of imports from China that could threaten their jobs.
quotes.speaker: United Auto Workers, DC Link
quotes.publication: UAW DC Link, archived by UNC Lobbying and Policy Change project

quotes.text: Adjustment in local labor markets is remarkably slow, with wages and labor-force participation rates remaining depressed and unemployment rates remaining elevated for at least a full decade after the China trade shock commences.
quotes.speaker: David H. Autor, David Dorn, Gordon H. Hanson
quotes.publication: NBER Working Paper 21906, The China Shock
